comparisons.peer_summary: Bank of America is subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, which requires periodic disclosure of privacy policies, allowing customers to opt out of information sharing with unaffiliated third parties, and mandating a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer records.
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs (GS) and Bank of America (BAC) disclose their obligations under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLB Act) and specifically address the intersection with Regulation S-P and customer information security. GS details the recent 2024 SEC amendments to Regulation S-P which mandate incident response programs and 30-day notification requirements for incidents involving sensitive customer information, with compliance deadlines extending to 2025 and 2026. BAC discloses its standing obligations under the GLB Act, noting the requirement to implement a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer records, but does not explicitly mention the new incident response and notification timelines associated with the specific 2024 Regulation S-P amendments in the provided text.

sentences.text: In 2024, the SEC amended Regulation S-P that implements the GLB Act.

The amendments to Regulation S-P require broker-dealers, investment companies and investment advisers registered with the SEC to adopt written policies and procedures for incident response programs to address unauthorized access to or use of customer information.
Larger covered entities, such as GS&Co., will have until December 2025, and smaller covered entities will have until June 2026, to comply with the amended Regulation S-P.

The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires us to periodically disclose Bank of America's privacy policies and practices relating to the disclosure of customer information and enables retail customers to opt out of our ability to share information with unaffiliated third parties, under certain circumstances.

The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and other laws also require us to implement a comprehensive information security program that includes administrative, technical and physical safeguards to provide the security and confidentiality of customer records and information.

comparisons.peer_topic: Regulation of specific subsidiaries and activities
comparisons.peer_summary: Broker-dealer subsidiaries are regulated by the SEC, FINRA, and NYSE; the futures commission merchant subsidiary by the CFTC and NFA; insurance activities by state agencies; and consumer financial products by the CFPB. Certain subsidiaries are registered as swap dealers with the CFTC and conditionally as security-based swap dealers with the SEC.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC have broker-dealer subsidiaries registered with the SEC, making them subject to the amended Regulation S-P. GS explicitly discloses the new requirements under these amendments, including the adoption of written incident response policies and the obligation to notify affected individuals within 30 days of an incident involving sensitive customer information. BAC’s disclosure outlines the general regulatory landscape for its broker-dealer subsidiaries, noting supervision by the SEC, FINRA, and NYSE, but does not mention the specific incident response and data breach notification mandates introduced by the 2024 Regulation S-P amendments.

sentences.text: The amendments to Regulation S-P require broker-dealers, investment companies and investment advisers registered with the SEC to adopt written policies and procedures for incident response programs to address unauthorized access to or use of customer information.

The amended Regulation S-P requires covered entities to notify within 30 days individuals affected by an incident involving sensitive customer information and provide them with details about the incident and other information intended to help affected individuals respond appropriately.

For instance, our broker-dealer subsidiaries are subject to both U.S. and international regulation, including supervision by the SEC, Financial Industry Regulatory Authority and New York Stock Exchange, among others; our futures commission merchant subsidiary supporting commodities and derivatives businesses in the U.S. is subject to regulation by and supervision of the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), National Futures Association, the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, and in the case of the Banks, certain banking regulators; our insurance activities are subject to licensing and regulation by state insurance regulatory agencies; and our consumer financial products and services are regulated by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
